cues.text: Sons in the Faith
Timothy , the son of a Greek father and a Jewish Christian mother named Eunice, was raised in the faith by his mother and grandmother Lois in Lystra, in Asia Minor.
When Paul passed through on his second missionary journey, he chose the young man as a companion, circumcising him first so that Timothy could move freely among Jewish communities.
Titus , by contrast, was a Gentile convert of Paul's own making, never required to be circumcised.
That distinction became, at the Council of Jerusalem, a test case for the Church's decision that Gentile converts need not adopt the full Mosaic Law.
Trusted Troubleshooters
Both men became Paul's most reliable agents for the Church's hardest problems.
Titus was dispatched to the fractious congregation at Corinth to mend a painful rift with the Apostle.
Later, he organized collections for the poor of Jerusalem, work Paul praised by calling him "my partner and fellow worker" among the Corinthians.

Timothy, meanwhile, was sent again and again as Paul's personal representative to troubled or young churches, from Thessalonica to Corinth to Philippi, carrying the Apostle's authority and settling disputes in his name.
Bishops of Ephesus and Crete
According to the Pastoral Epistles and early Church tradition, Timothy was left in charge of the church at Ephesus , and Titus of the church in Crete .
Each was entrusted with appointing qualified elders, correcting false teaching, and safeguarding sound doctrine in Paul's absence.
These instructions cover qualifications for bishops and deacons, right conduct in worship, and resistance to heresy.
They make the pastoral letters some of the earliest surviving evidence for how local church leadership was structured in the first generation after the Apostles.
The Only Personal Epistles
Of all Paul's letters, only two — First and Second Timothy — and one more — Titus — are addressed not to a community but to an individual disciple, giving them a uniquely personal and paternal tone.
Paul calls Timothy his "true child in the faith" , urging him not to let anyone despise his youth.
In what tradition holds were his final written words before execution in Rome, he asks Timothy to come quickly and bring his books and parchments.
Later Years and Deaths
Ancient tradition, reflected in the Roman Martyrology, holds that Timothy served as bishop of Ephesus into extreme old age.
It also holds that a pagan mob mortally beat him for opposing an idolatrous festival procession — some accounts say the festival of Artemis — probably under Domitian or Nerva.
Titus is said to have continued as bishop in Crete until his own death there in old age, and tradition remembers Titus as having died peacefully.
Legacy
Timothy and Titus stand at the head of the long line of bishops.
The Church holds that these bishops received their authority in unbroken succession from the Apostles themselves.
St. Irenaeus and others cited them as early witnesses precisely because of their documented, personal link to Paul.
Pope Benedict XVI, reflecting on their example, observed that they teach the Church "to serve the Gospel with generosity, knowing that this also involves a service to the Church itself."
